description: Complete computer graphics knowledge from fundamentals to cutting-edge research — written for a 15-year-old who wants to become a graphics programmer

topics.title: Real-Time Rendering Basics
topics.subtitle: How your screen turns triangles into pictures 60 times per second
topics.explanation_simple: Imagine you're drawing a 3D scene on a piece of paper, but instead of drawing it once, you have to draw it 60 times every second. Real-time rendering is the art of doing that fast enough that the picture moves smoothly. The main technique is called rasterization: it is like taking a wireframe 3D model and filling in all the pixels one by one, figuring out what color each tiny dot on your screen should be.
key_concepts: Graphics Pipeline — the assembly line that processes every triangle
Vertices vs Pixels — 3D points versus screen dots
Frame Buffer — the final image stored in memory
Swap Chain — double-buffering so you never see a half-drawn frame
V-Sync — synchronizing with your monitor refresh rate

subtopics.name: What is Rasterization?
subtopics.explanation_simple: Your screen is a grid of millions of tiny dots called pixels. Rasterization is the process of figuring out which pixels are covered by a triangle, then coloring them in. Think of it like coloring by numbers: you have a triangle shape defined by 3 corner points, and you need to fill in every square of a giant grid that falls inside that triangle. The computer does this millions of times per frame.
subtopics.how_it_works: For each triangle, the rasterizer looks at the 3 screen-space positions. It finds the bounding box (smallest rectangle that contains the triangle), then checks each pixel in that box to see if it is inside the triangle using edge functions. If a pixel is inside, it gets a fragment: a potential pixel that will go through more processing before becoming final.
subtopics.analogy: Like using a stencil: you cut out a triangle shape, lay it on graph paper, and color in all the squares you can see through the hole.

subtopics.name: The Graphics Pipeline — Complete Walkthrough
subtopics.explanation_simple: The graphics pipeline is like a factory assembly line. Raw 3D data goes in one end, and a finished 2D image comes out the other. Each stage does one specific job, and they all run in parallel: while one triangle is being rasterized, another is being transformed, and another is having its colors calculated. This parallelism is why GPUs are so fast.

stages.description: Reads vertex data (positions, colors, texture coordinates) from memory buffers and assembles them into triangles. Not programmable: it is fixed hardware.
A small program that runs once per vertex. It transforms 3D positions into screen coordinates, usually using matrix math (model, view, projection). You write this code yourself.
stages.what_you_can_do: Vertex skinning for animation, morph targets, procedural vertex displacement

stages.description: Optional stage that subdivides triangles into smaller triangles. Hull Shader decides HOW to subdivide, Tessellator does the actual splitting (fixed function), Domain Shader positions the new vertices. Great for making low-poly models look smooth.

Optional stage that runs once per triangle and can add or remove vertices. Can turn a point into a billboard quad, or a triangle into a fan of triangles. Rarely used in modern engines: compute shaders do this better.

The fixed-function stage that converts triangles into fragments (potential pixels). Determines which pixels the triangle covers, interpolates vertex data (colors, UVs, normals) across the surface using barycentric coordinates.
stages.diagram: Screen-space triangle -> [Rasterizer] -> Fragments with interpolated data

stages.description: Runs once per fragment (potential pixel). Calculates the final color based on textures, lighting, shadows, etc. This is where the visual magic happens.
stages.what_you_can_do: Per-pixel lighting, texture sampling, normal mapping, procedural patterns

stages.description: Combines the fragment shader result with the existing frame buffer. Handles depth testing, stencil testing, and blending (transparency). Fixed function plus some configurable settings.
stages.diagram: Fragment color + depth -> [OM] -> Frame buffer pixel

minimal_vertex_shader_glsl.description: The simplest possible vertex shader: transforms position using model-view-projection matrix

minimal_fragment_shader_glsl.description: Colors every pixel solid red: the hello world of shaders

simple_graphics_loop_concept.description: Pseudocode showing the per-frame rendering loop

learning_path.week_1: Understand the pipeline conceptually. Draw a triangle with OpenGL or DirectX.
learning_path.week_2: Learn matrix transformations (model, view, projection). Rotate a cube.
learning_path.week_3: Add texturing. Load an image file and map it onto your cube.

glossary.Alpha: The transparency channel of a color (0=transparent, 1=opaque)
glossary.Anisotropic Filtering: Texture filtering technique that reduces blurring on surfaces viewed at shallow angles
glossary.BRDF: Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function: describes how light reflects off a surface
glossary.BVH: Bounding Volume Hierarchy: a tree structure that accelerates ray intersection tests
glossary.Compute Shader: A shader that performs general-purpose calculations, not tied to graphics
glossary.Depth Buffer: A texture storing the distance of each pixel from the camera, used for visibility testing
glossary.Draw Call: A CPU command telling the GPU to render a set of geometry
glossary.Fragment: A potential pixel: a fragment may be discarded by depth testing or stencil testing
glossary.Frustum: The pyramid-shaped volume visible to the camera
glossary.G-Buffer: A set of textures in deferred rendering storing per-pixel geometry data
glossary.GI: Global Illumination: simulation of indirect light bouncing between surfaces
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: specialized processor for parallel graphics computation
glossary.HLSL: High-Level Shader Language: Microsoft shader language for DirectX
glossary.GLSL: OpenGL Shading Language: shader language for OpenGL and Vulkan
glossary.HDR: High Dynamic Range: storing color values beyond the 0-1 range
glossary.LOD: Level of Detail: using simpler geometry/textures for distant objects
glossary.MIP Map: Pre-computed, smaller versions of a texture for distant objects
glossary.MRT: Multiple Render Targets: rendering to several textures simultaneously
glossary.MSAA: Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing: sampling multiple positions per pixel to smooth edges
glossary.Normal Mapping: Using a texture to simulate surface detail by perturbing normals
glossary.PBR: Physically Based Rendering: lighting model based on real physics
glossary.PCF: Percentage Closer Filtering: softens shadow edges by sampling multiple points
glossary.SSAO: Screen Space Ambient Occlusion: approximates ambient occlusion from the depth buffer
glossary.SIMT: Single Instruction Multiple Threads: GPU execution model
glossary.TAA: Temporal Anti-Aliasing: uses previous frames to smooth edges
glossary.Tone Mapping: Converting HDR color values to displayable 0-1 range
glossary.VSync: Vertical Synchronization: synchronizes frame rate with monitor refresh rate
glossary.Warp: A group of 32 threads executing in lockstep on NVIDIA GPUs
